title: Momentum Stealers
author: We Made People
summary: The author names a recurring leadership challenge: the 'momentum stealer,' someone who is excited by the energy surrounding a mission but not actually committed to that specific mission, and who tries to redirect its momentum toward their own priorities. Using examples from family life (a spouse redirecting a garage-cleaning day toward the attic), business (pressure to launch a new product while the current one still has market share to capture), and church life (pressure to broaden a clearly defined confessional mission), the piece argues momentum stealers usually aren't malicious, just uncommitted to the specific mission at hand. It concludes that one of leadership's primary responsibilities is repeatedly restating the mission and calmly declining well-meaning redirection, since building anything substantial requires focus, and focus always requires saying no to good ideas that aren't the mission.
points: A 'momentum stealer' is excited by the energy around a mission, not the mission itself, and tries to redirect that energy toward their own priorities.
Momentum stealers usually aren't bad actors — many are sincere and well-intentioned but simply not committed to your specific mission.
Distinguish real reasons to pivot a mission (it was flawed, or success has earned the right to broaden it) from letting every enthusiastic outsider redefine your purpose.
One of leadership's primary jobs is to repeatedly restate the mission, which functions as a way of enforcing boundaries without conflict.
Building anything substantial requires focus, and focus always requires saying no to good ideas that simply aren't your mission.
quotes: A momentum stealer is someone who appears excited about your mission, but is actually more excited about the energy surrounding it.
What excites them is that something is finally moving, and they want to harness that movement for their own priorities.
Those people aren’t actually excited about our mission. They’re excited about the general idea of what we’re doing
One of the primary responsibilities of leadership is simply restating the mission over and over again.
Building anything meaningful requires focus. And focus always requires saying “no” to good ideas that aren’t your mission.
